The purpose of this study is to investigate the electrochemical properties of the $\mathbf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathbf { M o } _ { x }$ high-entropy alloys in three aqueous environments which simulate acidic, marine, and basic environments at ambient temperature (-25 -C). The potentiodynamic polarisation curves of the ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathsf { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys, obtained in aqueous solutions of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ and NaOH, clearly revealed that the corrosion resistance of the Mo-free alloy was superior to that of the Mo-containing alloys. On the other hand, the lack of hysteresis in cyclic polarisation tests and SEM micrographs confirmed that the Mo-containing alloys are not susceptible to pitting corrosion in NaCl solution.

1. Introduction

In the past, the development of conventional alloy systems has been based primarily on one principal element, such as iron-, aluminium-, magnesium-, and nickel-based alloys, limiting the number of applicable alloy systems, even though a substantial amount of other elements is incorporated for property/processing enhancement [1,2]. In the 1990s, Inoue et al. [3] obtained the highly glass forming alloy by using at least three different elements with significantly different atomic radii. In addition, Greer [4] came up with the ‘‘confusion principle” in which he stated that the possibility of crystallisation could be lowered if the number of alloying elements was large. In the last two decades, a wide range of multicomponent amorphous alloys, including titanium-, nickel-, zirconium-, iron-, cobalt-, and copper-based alloy [5–10] systems have been developed. Multiple studies have been widely investigated the corrosion and passivation behaviour of these multicomponent amorphous alloys in a variety of electrolytes [11–34]. However, the design concept of afore-mentioned multicomponent amorphous alloys was, once again, based on one principal element. In an attempt to break through the cognitive realm of alloy design, a new multicomponent amorphous alloy system was subsequently developed [35–39]. This new alloy system is also called ‘‘high-entropy alloys” which are composed of multiprincipal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. Each element in the alloy system is no more than 35 atomic percent (atom%). This study focuses on a new alloy design with multiprincipal elements in nonequimolar ratios.

Solid solutions with multiprincipal elements tend to be more stable because they have larger mixing entropies. Following Boltzmann’s hypothesis of the relationship between entropy and system complexity, the configurational entropy change per mole, $\Delta S _ { \mathrm { c o n f } } ,$ during the formation of a solid solution from six elements with equimolar fractions may be calculated from the following equation:

where k is the Boltzmann’s constant, x is the number of ways of mixing, and R is the gas constant, 8.314 J/mol/K. For instance, $\Delta S _ { \mathrm { c o n f } }$ of equimolar alloys with 3, 5, 7, and 9 elements are 1.10 R, 1.61 R, 1.95 R, and 2.20 R, respectively. In fact, when other positive vibrational, electronic, and magnetic contributions are considered, the entropy change associated with mixing in equimolar high-entropy alloy is greater than the calculated one [40]. Under the effects of high mixing entropies and the accompanied sluggish cooperative diffusion, they easily yield the formation of simple solid-solution phases and nanostructures during solidification, rather than many binary and ternary intermetallic compounds or other complicated phases [4,40]. The simplification of their structures avoids the disadvantages of difficulty in microstructure analyses and the inherent brittleness of ordered compounds.

According to previous studies [35–39,41–45], these high-entropy alloy systems possess the following specialties: (1) ease of amorphisation and nanoprecipitation in the alloy, (2) thermal stability, (3) high hardness [Vickers hardness $( \mathrm { H V } ) = 7 0 0 ]$ , (4) superior corrosion resistance, (5) excellent resistance to anneal softening, wear $[ 1 . 2 - 1 . 8 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { m } \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 } ]$ and oxidation. Additionally, coating technology was further expanding their range of application, to include the hard-facing of golf heads and rollers [46], diffusion barrier [47], and soft magnetic films [48]. Among those previous studies, Reference 45 pointed out that $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ with various Mo contents (x values in the molar ratio, $x = 0 { - } 1 . 0 )$ is ductile, work hardenable, and strong at high temperature up to $8 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ , indicating that this alloy has potential application in high-temperature structures and working tools. However, the corrosion characteristics of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \boldsymbol { x } } }$ alloys are relatively unknown. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to investigate the electrochemical behaviour of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys under different environmental conditions.

2. Experimental
2.1. Test material

Elements cobalt (Co), chromium (Cr), titanium (Ti), iron (Fe), and nickel (Ni) with purities of over 99 wt.% were present as granules as raw materials. The 39.5 wt.% Fe–60.5 wt.% Mo master alloy was used with the added molybdenum (Mo). This high-entropy alloy is a six-component alloy in the form of $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x } ,$ with 1.5 mol of Co, Ni, 0.5 mol of Ti, and 1 mol of the other two alloying elements and between zero and 1 mol of the added Mo. Table 1 presents the chemical compositions of the alloys in weight percent (wt.%). The multiprincipal-element $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloy system with various Mo contents with x from 0 to 1.0 was prepared in this work. An induction furnace was used to melt the high-entropy alloys at $1 6 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ after purging with argon. First, raw materials of Co, Fe, and Ni were placed in the crucible. When Co, Fe, and Ni had melted in liquid state, then ${ \mathrm { T i } } , \subset { \mathrm { r } } ,$ and FeMo were added to the crucible in order according to their melting points. Finally, the melt was poured into a shell mold preheated at $1 1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C .$ The size of the ingots was $8 \times 7 \times 1 4$ (cm). The high-entropy alloy cylinder for electrochemical measurements was obtained by cutting the bulk material by electric arc line into pieces that were 3 mm thick and 8 mm in diameter. Each test specimen was then cold mounted, using an epoxy resin to give an exposed surface area of $0 . 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for the high-entropy alloys. Before each electrochemical experiment, all specimens were mechanically ground using a series of 240–600 silicon carbide (SiC) grit papers and cleaned with acetone and distilled water.
2.2. Structure analysis of the $C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { x }$ alloy

The microstructure and composition analyses of the as-cast alloys were carried out by JEOL 5410 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS). X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Cu Ka radiation was used to identify crystalline phases and obtain the lattice parameters of these alloys. The XRD investigation was performed with the diffraction angle (2h) from $2 0 ^ { \circ }$ to 100- at a speed of 4-/min.
2.3. Electrochemical measurements

The corrosion resistance of $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys was conducted in three different environmental conditions; 1 molar concentration (M) sodium hydroxide (NaOH), 0.5 M sulfuric acid $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 } \mathrm { ) }$ , and 1 M sodium chloride (NaCl), which will be referred to as base, acid, and salt solution, respectively henceforth at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ under atmospheric pressure. The test solution was deaerated by bubbling purified nitrogen gas before and throughout the electrochemical tests to eliminate the effect of dissolved oxygen. The electrochemical polarisation was performed in a typical three electrode cell that consisted of a specimen as the working electrode, a silver/silver chloride $( \mathsf { A g } / \mathsf { A g C l } )$ in 3 M potassium chloride (KCl) as the reference electrode, and a platinum (Pt) sheet as the counter electrode. The Ag/AgCl scale (3 M KCl) is 0.208 V lower than the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) [49]:
Unless otherwise stated in this paper, all potentials recorded were referred to standard hydrogen electrode.

Potentiodynamic polarisation measurements were made at a scan rate of 1 mV/s from an initial potential of 0.5 V to a final potential of 1.5 V versus the open current potential (OCP). The potential was controlled and the current was measured using a potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT30). A cyclic polarisation technique started at 0.5 V by scanning at 1 mV/s towards more positive potentials up to 1.5 V versus the OCP, at which value the potential scan was reversed and returned to where the polarisation began. Before either of these tests was conducted, the OCP was recorded for 15 min to yield a steady-state potential. Then, the specimen was cathodically polarised to a potential of $- 1 9 2 \mathrm { m V } _ { \mathrm { S H E } }$ for 5 min to reduce the existing surface films. Following electrochemical testing, multiple electrochemical parameters were determined: $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } } ,$ corrosion potential, i.e., the potential where zero current density [21]; $E _ { \mathrm { p p } } ,$ primary passivation potential, the potential at which the maximum anodic current density reached in the active region [50]; $E _ { \mathrm { s p } } ,$ secondary passivation potential, the potential at which the maximum anodic current density reached in the passive region [51]; $E _ { \mathbf { b } } ,$ the potential at which the current density suddenly increases is determined to be the breakdown potential [20]; DE, the difference between $E _ { \mathrm { b } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { p p } }$ is the estimated passive region width [42]; $E _ { \mathrm { p r o t } } ,$ the protection potential where the forward and reverse scan crosses in the passive region [51]; $E _ { \mathrm { r p } } ,$ the repassivation potential is considered to be the potential at which the cyclic polarisation curves are approximately horizontal on the potential reverse scan [42]; $i _ { \mathrm { c r i } } ,$ critical current density, the maximum anodic current density in the active region [50]; $i _ { \mathrm { p a s s } } ,$ anodic current density values remain completely constant in the passive range [50]; the corrosion current density, i<sub>corr</sub>, is obtained from the curves using the intersection of the cathodic linear extrapolation (approximately 50 to 100 mV from the corrosion potential) and the corrosion potential horizontal line.

2.4. Surface morphology and chemical analysis

Following the polarisation experiment, the specimen was cleaned using distilled water and then dried in nitrogen. Immediately thereafter, the morphology and chemical composition of the corroded surface of the high-entropy alloy was investigated using a JEOL 5410 SEM.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Microstructure of the as-cast $C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { x }$ alloys

Fig. 1 illustrates the XRD patterns of the as-cast ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathsf { C r F e } } .$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x } \left( x = 0 , 0 . 1 , 0 . 5 , 0 . 8 \right)$ alloys. In this study, all these alloys basically belong to a simple FCC solid-solution structure. However, as Mo content in $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \lambda } }$ alloys increases up to 0.5 and 0.8 mol, the small peaks slightly on the left and right of the matrix FCC in XRD patterns are identified as Cr and Mo rich sigma (r) phase. 3.2. Potentiodynamic polarisation curves

text: The addition of Mo is widely recognised for its beneficial effect on the corrosion resistance of the stainless steels and has been studied extensively in the literature [60–65]. Sugimoto and Sawada [60] concluded that Mo addition to austenitic stainless steels allows formation of a passive film consisted of a Cr (III) oxyhydroxide containing ${ \mathrm { M o } } ^ { 6 + }$ ions, which reduces the corrosion current density in the active region for acidic solution. However, Hashimoto et al. [61] proposed that the main effect of Mo was to decrease the rate of dissolution in active zones by formation and retention of Mo (VI) oxyhydroxide or molybdate $( \mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - } )$ at these sites. Furthermore, Ogawa et al. [62] suggested that Mo is first dissolved from the substrate into the solution and then oxidised to $\mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$

As mentioned above, many authors conclude that molybdenum species, present in the passive layer, are mainly ionic compounds $( \mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - } )$ , which are adsorbed on the top of the material surface, acting as a barrier against the electrochemical attack [63–67]. However, given the 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ acidic conditions (pH < 1) in this study and according to Pourbaix diagrams [68], an influence of Mo via $\mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ formation should be considered improbable, since, in these conditions, MoO<sup>2</sup> is unstable thermodynamically and tends to precipitate as Mo (VI) oxide, e.g., $\mathrm { { \bf M o O } } _ { 3 } .$ . text: The obtained polarisation results (Table 4) have revealed that Mo addition tends to increase the corrosion current density of Mo-containing alloys in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } .$ These results are in disagreement with Hashimoto [69] who reported that in the active region of stainless steels, where preferential dissolution of iron and chromium occurred, the formation of the passive molybdenum oxide film was responsible for a large decrease of the current density. The opposite results were found by Bojinov et al. [70] in studies of the electrochemical behaviour of anodic films on pure Cr,

Fe–Cr alloys and Fe–Cr–Mo alloys in 1 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution. The corrosion current density in the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 1 } }$ alloy is lower than that in the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 }$ alloy, which may be attributed to the simultaneous presence of lower Cr and slightly higher Mo content (1.8 atom%) in the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 1 } }$ alloy (Table 2). As the Mo content increases from 0.5 to 0.8 mol in the high-entropy alloys, the interdendrite phase of the ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys is a Cr and Mo rich r phase, and the dendrite is a Cr and Mo depleted phase. The r phase is probably the most studied and undesirable phase in a stainless steel. Formation of r phase can occur in the austenitic, ferritic, and duplex stainless steels. Especially in duplex stainless steels, the formation of r phase is accelerated by increased amount of Cr and Mo [71,72]. The formation of that phase not only causes losses in ductility and toughness of the steel, but also reduces its corrosion resistance by removing Cr and Mo from the austenitic matrix [73]. Conejero et al. [57] studied premature corrosion failure of a 316L stainless steel plate exposed to a $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ environment. It was reported that a 316L stainless steel plate has failed due to the presence of r phase, which is deleterious to corrosion performance of the stainless steels in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution. Therefore, the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ $\left( x = 0 . 5 , 0 . 8 \right)$ alloys possessed the lower corrosion current density in comparison with the Mo-free alloy in this study, which could be also attributed to the presence of r phase.

3.3. Cyclic potentiodynamic polarisation

A cyclic polarisation technique was adopted to determine whether the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys $( x = 0 , 0 . 1 , 0 . 5 ,$ and 0.8)

suffered from pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution at approximately 25 -C. The hysteresis revealed by the cyclic polarisation curve provides information on the pitting corrosion rate and how readily a passive film repairs itself. Negative hysteresis occurs when the reverse scan current density is less than that for the forward scan, and positive hysteresis occurs when the reverse scan current density exceeds the forward scan current density [75].

Cyclic polarisation measurements were made at a scanning rate of 1 mV/s. The potential scan began at 0.5 V and continued in the anodic direction until the potential was 1.5 V versus the OCP, at which value the potential scan was reversed and returned to where the polarisation began. Fig. 5 plots the cyclic polarisation curves of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \chi } }$ alloys with various Mo contents $\begin{array} { r } { ( x = 0 , } \end{array}$ 0.1, 0.5, and 0.8). The black and gray arrows next to the forward and reverse anodic branches indicate the potential scan directions. In terms of the electrochemical parameters shown in Table 6, the addition of Mo moves the $E _ { \mathrm { b } }$ in the noble direction. The cyclic polarisation curve of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 }$ alloy was referred to as a pseudo-passive curve because the curve did not exhibit a distinct $E _ { \mathbf { p } \mathbf { p } } ,$ but the $E _ { \mathrm { b } }$ was observed. The difference between $E _ { \mathrm { b } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { p p } }$ was the estimated passive region width DE. The DE for the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 }$ alloy was 557 mV. As the Mo content in the $\mathbf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathbf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys increased from 0.1 to 0.8 mol, the DE varied between 1371 and 1429 mV. Therefore, the DE of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys broadened due to the effect of Mo, which is in agreement with Sedriks et al. [58]. The ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys $\left( x = 0 . 1 , 0 . 5 , \right.$ and 0.8) alloys showed negative hysteresis in the cyclic polarisation curve, indicating that the Mo-containing alloys were resistant to pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution, as can be seen in Fig. 5b–d. However, the positive hysteresis of the cyclic polarisation curve demonstrates that pitting of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 }$ alloy can be induced in 1 M NaCl solution, as in Fig. ${ \it 5 } ( { \mathrm { a } } ) .$ . The area contained within a positive hysteresis loop is related to the amount of pit propagation that occurs during the cycle, according to Wilde [76]. The intersection at the passive region defined protection potential $( E _ { \mathrm { p r o t } } ) ,$ , below which the established pits on metal surface apparently could not keep on growing. In contrast, new pits would initiate only above $E _ { \mathrm { b } } .$ Between $E _ { \mathrm { p r o t } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { b } } ,$ new pits could not initiate, but old ones still could grow. Furthermore, the $i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ of the Mo-containing alloys was lower than that of the Mo-free alloy. Therefore, adding Mo element has positive effect on the corrosion resistance of ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys in 1 M NaCl solution.

It has been well established that the addition of Mo to stainless steels improves the pitting corrosion resistance in media containing chloride [50,58,77–78]. It has been considered that Mo could form $\mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ ions in the solid state in the outer regions of the film in neutral NaCl solutions according to Pourbaix diagrams [68]. This $\mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ layer is cation selective and can serve as a very effective pitting inhibitor, which resists the incorporation of anions such as Cl<sup></sup> and $\mathsf { B r } ^ { - }$ , allowing for the growth of the Cr oxide inner barrier layer. The resulting bipolar layer stabilises the oxide phase [65].

For Fe–Ni–Cr–Mo stainless steel, such as 316 stainless steels, the relative effectiveness of Cr and Mo contents on pitting or crevice corrosion usually can be assessed qualitatively by pitting resistance equivalent (PRE), which is represented by the empirical equation [82]:

In this study, according to the PRE equation mentioned above, the PRE values for the pitting-resistant $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 1 } }$ $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 5 } ,$ , and $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 8 }$ alloys are 26.32, 59.05, and 79.31, respectively. The $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 } } ,$ alloy, which is susceptible to pitting corrosion, has PRE value 16.87. This indicates that a PRE of above 26 is crucial to protect the as-cast Mo-containing alloys from pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution.

The obtained polarisation results (Table 6) have shown that the Mo-containing alloys exhibit lower corrosion current density than that of the Mo-free alloy, which is in agreement with the other authors [50,58,77–78]. However, the corrosion current density of the Mo-containing alloys decreases as the Mo content increases from 0.1 to 0.8 mol. Although the PRE value for the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 3 } }$ 8 is the highest among the Mo-containing alloys, the corrosion current density is the lowest among the Mo-containing alloys. The major drawbacks of the PRE equation in using parameters based on Cr and Mo contents is that they ignored the relationship between microstructure and pitting corrosion resistance. Kim et al. [83] investigated corrosion of r phase formation of 25% Cr duplex stainless steel (DSS) in 4 M NaCl solutions. According to the author, the increase ofMo content in DSS has been reported to promote formation of r phase, leading to a reduction in pitting corrosion resistance of the DSS. Similar results were found by Cvijovic´ and Radenkovic´ [84] in studies ofthe microstructure and pitting corrosion resistance of the annealed DSS in 0.5 M NaCl solution. In this study, as the Mo content increases from 0.5 to 0.8 mol in the high-entropy alloys, the interdendrite phase of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \boldsymbol { x } } }$ alloys is a Cr and Mo rich r phase, and the dendrite is a Cr and Mo depleted phase. Mo and Cr contents are higher in the interdendrite than in the dendrite, as can be observed in Table 2. The PRE value and the associated resistance to pitting may become notably different in the two phases. Therefore, the formation of r phase in the ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathsf { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x } ( x = 0 . 5 ,$ , and 0.8) alloys can result in a significant degradation of pitting corrosion resistance in 1 M NaCl solutions.

A passive film is generally believed to repair itself when the repassivation potential $( E _ { \mathrm { r p } } )$ exceeds the corrosion potential. As listed in Table 6, the $E _ { \mathrm { r p } }$ is more noble than the $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } } ,$ regardless of whether Mo is incorporated. Therefore, the addition of appropriate Mo to $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys improves the ability to restore its passive film.
3.4. SEM photomicrographs of corroded surfaces

Fig. 6 presents the SEM microstructure of the ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathsf { C r F e } } .$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys after potentiodynamic polarisation in deaerated $0 . 5 \mathrm { ~ M ~ } \mathrm { ~ H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } 0 _ { 4 } .$ According to the SEM images, surface examination showed that the major types of corrosion were mainly uniform corrosion. As the Mo content increases from 0.5 to 0.8 mol in the high-entropy alloys, according to the Table 2, the interdendrite phase of the $\mathbf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathbf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathbf { M o } _ { \lambda }$ alloys is a Cr and Mo rich phase, and the dendrite is a Cr and Mo depleted phase. The active dendrites are coupled to the Cr and Mo depleted and Cr and Mo rich passive interdendrites. The low anode/cathode surface area ratio results in galvanic corrosion at the dendrites, and the electrochemical action causes attack along the dendrites in Cr and Mo depleted alloys. To verify the composition of the interdendrite phase, the EDS analysis was used, and the result is listed in Table 7. There are two areas, designated A and B in Fig. 6c after the potentiodynamic polarisation of the alloy $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 5 }$ in deaerated 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ . Area A is the interdendrite and area B is the dendrite. The EDS analysis demonstrates that the interdendrites of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 5 }$ alloy are rich in Cr and Mo, but poor in Co, Ni, and Fe. Especially, the atomic percent of Mo in the interdendrites (23.9 atom%) considerably exceeds that in the dendrites (6.4 atom%) in the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 5 }$ alloy. Therefore, the corrosion on the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys $( x = 0 . 5$ , and 0.8) alloys was concentrated to the dendrites.

text: The SEM micrographs of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \chi } }$ alloys after potentiodynamic polarisation in deaerated 1 M NaCl are shown in Fig. 7. The corroded surfaces of the Mo-free alloy showed that the major types of corrosion were mainly pitting corrosion, not uniform corrosion. It is observed that several pits formed in 1 M NaCl on Mo-free alloy. Moreover, we find that there are no pits on the surface of Mo-containing alloys, supporting the previous finding that Mo-containing alloys are free of pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution. It appears, therefore, that the Mo-free alloy is more susceptible to pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution than the Mo-containing alloys. These results are in agreement with the cyclic polarisation curves as presented in Fig. 5.

Fig. 8a–d illustrates the SEM microstructure of the ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys after potentiodynamic polarisation in deaerated 1 M NaOH. It is clear that the corrosion mode in NaOH is more of general type, indicating passivating nature of the alloys in this oxidising solution. The pit-like contrasts on the ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathrm { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys $( x = 0 , 0 . 1 , 0 . 5 $ , and 0.8) alloys are due to the microporosities formed during the casting and the mechanical polishing effect, compared to Fig. 2, images of the as-cast ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys with various Mo contents. The surface of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ alloys $( x = 0 . 1 , 0 . 5$ , and 0.8) alloys is roughened by general corrosion. Similar results were found by Mondal et al. [22] in the studies of the electrochemical behaviour of multicomponent amorphous and nanocrystalline zirconium (Zr)-based alloys in different environments, which demonstrated that pitting has occurred in the alloy in NaCl solutions whereas no pitting has observed in NaOH and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solutions.
5. Conclusions

The electrochemical characteristics of the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ high-entropy alloys in solutions of 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } , \ 1$ M NaCl, and NaOH have been studied in this paper. The potentiodynamic polarisation curves of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \lambda } }$ alloys in acidic solution exhibit active–passive corrosion behaviour, yielding an extensive passive region. The corrosion current density and passive current density of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } }$ alloy are significantly lower than those of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 0 . 5 } T i _ { 1 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 1 } , C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { 0 . 5 } , }$ and $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 . 8 }$ alloys. Therefore, the Mo-free alloy is more resistant to general corrosion than that of the Mo-containing alloys in acidic environments. On the other hand, the cyclic polarisation curves indicate that the Mo-free alloy tends to pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution accounting for the lower breakdown potential and narrower range of potentials in the passive region. Additionally, the negative hysteresis in the reverse scans of the cyclic polarisation curves and SEM images show that the Mo-containing alloys are not susceptible to pitting corrosion in deaerated 1 M NaCl solution in this study, and that the passive film is generally believed to repair itself. It is revealed that the addition of Mo in the ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1 . 5 } { \mathrm { C r F - } }$ $\mathbf { e N i } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { \lambda }$ alloys improves the pitting resistance in chloride environments, in that the breakdown potential for the Mo-containing alloys are much higher than that for the Mo-free alloy. Potentiodynamic polarisation curves of the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1 . 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1 . 5 } T i _ { 0 . 5 } M o _ { \chi } }$ alloys, obtained in 1 M NaOH solution, clearly reveal that the corrosion resistance decreases with the Mo content increases.
